sentences.text: The holotype, which is the specific specimen the species is based on, is a single cervical vertebra measuring between 77 and 78 cm in length.
This animal possessed extremely hollow and lightly built bones adapted for soaring flight, making it one of the largest azhdarchids, comparable in size to Quetzalcoatlus and Hatzegopteryx.
Initial estimates placed its wingspan between 11 and 13 meters, suggesting it was the largest known pterosaur, though recent research suggests the wingspan was between 8 and 10 meters.
In 1943, a railway worker discovered fossil fragments including an incomplete cervical vertebra measuring 60.96 cm during phosphate mining near Ruseifa, Jordan.
In 1954, Camille Arambourg misidentified the holotype vertebra as a wing metacarpal, leading to the 1959 naming of Titanopteryx philadelphiae.
Paleontologist Camille Arambourg described the specimen as a new genus and species, Titanopteryx philadelphiae, in 1959.
In 1989, paleontologist Lev Nessov renamed the genus from Titanopteryx to Arambourgiania to honor Camille Arambourg.
Frey and Martill extrapolated the total neck length of the holotype to be about 3 meters.
In the late 1990s, Frey and Martill estimated the wingspan of Arambourgiania to be between 11 and 13 meters based on a 1.18 ratio.
In 2003, researchers suggested the wingspan of Arambourgiania was likely about 7 meters, though they provided no rationale for this estimate.
Arambourgiania is classified as a member of the pterosaur family Azhdarchidae.
In 1984, Nessov assigned Arambourgiania, then known as Titanopteryx, to the subfamily Azhdarchinae.
In 1986, Kevin Padian declared his family Titanopterygiidae a junior synonym of Azhdarchinae after realizing the cervical vertebrae diagnoses were identical.
Recent studies consistently classify Arambourgiania as a derived azhdarchid in the subfamily Quetzalcoatlinae, though its exact phylogenetic position remains disputed.
Arambourgiania lived during the Late Cretaceous period, specifically the Maastrichtian age, inhabiting Jordan approximately 72 to 66 million years ago.
Fossils of Arambourgiania in Jordan are found in the Ruseifa Formation, which represents a deep marine environment from the Maastrichtian.
Fragments of cervical vertebrae attributed to Arambourgiania have been found in Jordan and the United States.
In 1975, Douglas A. Lawson concluded that the holotype specimen was a cervical vertebra rather than a wing metacarpal, correcting an earlier interpretation.
In 1995, David Martill and Eberhard Frey traveled to Jordan to locate the holotype and clarify the identity of Arambourgiania.
Fossil remains from the United States and Morocco have been tentatively assigned to Arambourgiania, though this classification is not certain.
A 2014 study suggests the endocasts referred to Arambourgiania by Lewy likely belong to birds due to their 3 cm length and bird-like structure.
